![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14253263/assets/7c8c3764dcdd63bb7f7078ccdb729a95712f788db25fc1ba048172fc06b2b3d1.png)

Find the total area bounded by the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we want to find the interval for $\theta $ that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $3\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
3\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}
$$

So, the first petal is traversed for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14253263/assets/75e6fabf01bb0a73e17efee8d9d52d7c1e66cfd78eccd3d5c4d1f9e087335c1f.png)

Since there are $3$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{total}} & =3\cdot {A}_{\text{petal}} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{(\theta +\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ))|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[(\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ))-(-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14253263/assets/53d86dd26966e3e4b5a75441fc7a1d6ab8f2244097f61677086f5783495ed6cb.png)

The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )$ is given by the integral

$$
A=\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?
questions.worked_solution:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with $5$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A=\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14253263/assets/53d86dd26966e3e4b5a75441fc7a1d6ab8f2244097f61677086f5783495ed6cb.png)

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=0$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{5},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{5}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{5}=0+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{5} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{5}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{2\pi }{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{5}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{2\pi }{5} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{2\pi }{5}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{3\pi }{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{7} & ={\theta }_{5}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{2\pi }{5}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{3\pi }{5} \\ {\theta }_{8} & ={\theta }_{6}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{3\pi }{5}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{4\pi }{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fifth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the fourth petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{9} & ={\theta }_{7}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{3\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{4\pi }{5} \\ {\theta }_{10} & ={\theta }_{8}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{4\pi }{5}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $5$ petals of our rose:

$$
{{[0,\frac{\pi }{5}]}_{⏟}}_{1\text{st}},\,{{[\frac{\pi }{5},\frac{2\pi }{5}]}_{⏟}}_{2\text{nd}},\,{{[\frac{2\pi }{5},\frac{3\pi }{5}]}_{⏟}}_{3\text{rd}},\,{{[\frac{3\pi }{5},\frac{4\pi }{5}]}_{⏟}}_{4\text{th}},\,{{[\frac{4\pi }{5},\pi ]}_{⏟}}_{5\text{th}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =0$ to $\theta =\pi :$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}=\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta 
$$

Find the total area bounded by the polar curve $r=\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ),$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we want to find the interval for $\theta $ that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $5\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$:

$$
5\theta =0,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =0,\frac{\pi }{5}
$$

As a result, the first petal is traversed for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{5}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14253263/assets/e41fe5bc79759e102339e1824d82691c45fb454a86b1ca4674b1d6ba5770c107.png)

Since there are $5$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{total}} & =5\cdot {A}_{\text{petal}} \\  & =5\cdot 3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =15\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(10\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{15}{2}{(\theta -\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10\theta ))|}_{0}^{\pi /5} \\  & =\frac{15}{2}[(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi ))-(0-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{15}{2}(\frac{\pi }{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})$ (shown above) is given by the integral

$$
A=2{\int }_{-3\pi /20}^{\pi /20}{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?
questions.worked_solution:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with $5$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A=2{\int }_{-3\pi /20}^{\pi /20}{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{3\pi }{20}$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{20},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{5}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{5}=-\frac{3\pi }{20}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{20} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{20}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{20}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{9\pi }{20}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{7} & ={\theta }_{5}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{9\pi }{20} \\ {\theta }_{8} & ={\theta }_{6}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{9\pi }{20}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{13\pi }{20}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fifth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{5}$ to both ends of the interval of the fourth petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{9} & ={\theta }_{7}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{9\pi }{20}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{13\pi }{20} \\ {\theta }_{10} & ={\theta }_{8}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{13\pi }{20}+\frac{\pi }{5}=\frac{17\pi }{20}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $5$ petals of our rose:

$$
{{[-\frac{3\pi }{20},\frac{\pi }{20}]}_{⏟}}_{1\text{st}},\,{{[\frac{\pi }{20},\frac{\pi }{4}]}_{⏟}}_{2\text{nd}},\,{{[\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{9\pi }{20}]}_{⏟}}_{3\text{rd}},\,{{[\frac{9\pi }{20},\frac{13\pi }{20}]}_{⏟}}_{4\text{th}},\,{{[\frac{13\pi }{20},\frac{17\pi }{20}]}_{⏟}}_{5\text{th}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{10}$ to $\theta =\frac{17\pi }{20}:$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}=2{\int }_{-3\pi /20}^{17\pi /20}{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta 
$$

Since there are $4$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{total}} & =4\cdot {A}_{\text{petal}} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =18\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =9{(\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =9[(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ))-(-\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))] \\  & =9(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$
